title: One step away
note: The tan-era version failed a blind pilot 4/4: every viewer read it as 'walking away toward the door', which is a different picture one activity over. The fix is that a still cannot show 'one step and no more' — an absence is unscoreable — so the claim is how CLOSE she still is to the bed. She is barely away from it. Two things added from the §5 and blind-pilot records in docs/pilot-prompts.md before the first restyle round. First, the winning tan-era formulation of 'barely away' was not an adjective but a geometry — trailing foot level with the bed's edge, bed at her heel, leading foot one pace ahead — because 'very close' is not something a reviewer can score and a foot position is. Second, §5 records that Lucy reads smaller and younger in this picture than anywhere else in the library, so her age and size are stated here specifically. No leash is deliberate and matches the alt text in js/content.js, which does not mention one; the later rungs walk the handler across the room, where a trailing black line would be an unreadable puddle against the floor.
scene: Interior entry hall, side view, camera at standing eye level. This is the same room, the same camera position and the same distance from the viewer as the other rungs of this ladder: Lucy's rectangular cool-grey dog bed on the left, the closed charcoal front door on the right, and a clear span of taupe-grey floor between them, with the whole walk from bed to door visible in frame. Lucy lies on the bed in a settled down — elbows and hips on the bed, front legs extended, head up and level, eyes on the handler, feet unmoved. She is a medium-large adult dog and must read as one: not small, not puppyish, the same size and age as in every other picture. Her size in frame, the bed's position and the camera never change between these pictures. No leash. The handler has taken a single step away from the bed and stopped. She is still very close to it, and the way to show that is the position of her feet: her trailing foot is still level with the near edge of the bed — the bed is at her heel, close enough to touch — and her leading foot is one pace ahead of it, no more. Her feet are apart because a step has been completed, but both are flat on the floor and her weight is even between them. There is far more floor between her and the door than between her and Lucy. Her body stays square to the bed rather than turned into a walk, and she is turned back toward Lucy, looking down at her. She is NOT mid-stride, not leaning toward the door, and not walking. The front door stays closed across the room, still far away.
mustBeTrue: the handler is still much closer to the bed than to the door — barely away from it — and is standing still with both feet planted and her weight even, turned back to look at Lucy rather than caught mid-stride.
